framing: Generative AI products have existed at commercial scale since late 2022. That is not enough history to identify a cycle in AI company profitability — three or four years of data can show a trend but cannot distinguish a trend from the upswing of a cycle. What follows uses the two capital cycles that do have history: semiconductors, which are the physical input, and the 1990s telecom buildout, which is the closest structural analogue. Neither is a forecast. Both are ways of asking what the current numbers would look like if this is the top.

telecom_buildout.label: US telecom fibre buildout, 1996–2002

cumulative_capex.note: Plus roughly $800B of M&A in 1999 alone.

unused_capacity_post_bust.note: Share of laid fibre still dark four years after the bust.

telecom_buildout.demand_forecast_error: The industry's governing belief was that internet traffic was doubling every 100 days, a WorldCom claim. Actual traffic doubled roughly once per year. The error was not in the direction of demand but in its rate, and the rate is what sized the buildout.
telecom_buildout.circular_revenue: Capacity swaps between carriers — A buys $100M from B while B buys $100M from A — booked revenue on both sides with no net cash movement. Equipment vendors including Lucent, Nortel and Cisco also financed customers who then bought their equipment.
telecom_buildout.aftermath: The overcapacity was real and so was the eventual use. Cheap abundant bandwidth by the mid-2000s is what made streaming video and the mobile internet economically possible. The infrastructure was not wasted; the equity was.

ai_buildout.label: AI data centre buildout, 2023–

capex_by_year.note: Four largest — Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta.
Five hyperscalers, including Oracle. J.P. Morgan's comparable estimate is $697B.

capex_share_of_us_gdp_2026.note: Derived: $725B against $32.48T US GDP. Roughly twice the telecom buildout's peak share of GDP, reached in about four years rather than five, and concentrated in fewer than ten companies rather than dozens.

global_ai_spending_2026.note: All AI categories, not just infrastructure. Up 44% year over year.

ai_buildout.ramp_duration: Roughly four years from the first generative AI product launches to peak annual investment — faster than the 1990s telecom buildout or the 2010s cloud expansion.

differences_that_matter.detail: The 1990s fibre builders were largely pre-revenue or thinly profitable. The hyperscalers fund most of their capex from operating cash flow generated by unrelated, highly profitable businesses. Debt/EBITDA under 1.5x is not a telecom balance sheet.

Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta were the beneficiaries of the fibre glut, not its victims. Their current executives lived through that cycle. That is either reassuring or an argument that they have priced the risk and accepted it.

Fibre in the ground held value for decades. GPUs depreciate in three to five years and are exposed to their own successor products. Underused fibre is a dormant asset; underused GPUs are a wasting one.

Fibre required consumers to first buy broadband access. AI is usable by anyone with an existing internet connection, which is why adoption curves are steeper. Adoption is not the same as willingness to pay at a price that covers cost.

The vendor-financing and capacity-swap patterns that inflated 1990s telecom revenue have partial modern analogues in chip vendors investing in their own customers and in cross-committed cloud contracts. Whether these are equivalent in kind is genuinely contested, not settled.

In 2000 the losses landed on public equity and bank loans. Today a large share of the marginal financing sits in private credit funds, insurers, pension vehicles and retail-facing products, where mark-to-market is slower and exposure is harder to observe. Slower price discovery is not less risk.

leading_indicators_to_watch: Memory pricing — DRAM and NAND prices and semiconductor operating margins are at levels that historically have not persisted.
Hyperscaler bond coverage ratios — reported to have fallen from roughly 5x in February 2026 to under 2x by July.
CoreWeave's GPU-collateralised facility, where repayment began January 2026 as collateral values declined.
Data centre ABS take-out capacity — a ~$25B market facing ~$300B of eventual refinancing need.
Oracle CDS spreads, the widest move among major tech names in 2026.
The gap between signed and commenced leases, currently ~$675B, and whether commencements track signings.
